sources.excerpt: Mar 2, 2023 · Only when MSG was linked to Chinese cuisine did Americans panic.

reasoning: Scientific consensus and rigorous double-blind, placebo-controlled studies have consistently disproven the claim that monosodium glutamate (MSG) causes the cluster of symptoms historically referred to as "Chinese restaurant syndrome" (such as headaches, numbness, weakness, and flushing) under normal dietary consumption. The term originated from a 1968 anecdotal letter published in the New England Journal of Medicine, which spurred widespread public concern despite lacking scientific evidence. Major health and regulatory organizations worldwide—including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the World Health Organization (WHO), and the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA)—classify MSG as "Generally Recognized as Safe" (GRAS). Furthermore, the glutamate in MSG is chemically indistinguishable from glutamate naturally found in foods like tomatoes, parmesan cheese, and mushrooms.
